Bug_Details:
Comparison using reference equality instead of value equality. Reference equality of boxed primitive types is usually not useful, as they are value objects, and it is bug-prone, as instances are cached for some values but not others. Comparison using reference equality instead of value equality. The inputs to
this comparison are boxed primitive types, where reference equality is
particularly bug-prone: Primitive wrapper classes cache instances for some (but
usually not all) values, so == may be equivalent to equals() for some values but
not others. Additionally, not all versions of the runtime and other libraries
use the cache in the same cases, so upgrades may change behavior. Furthermore,
reference identity is usually not useful for primitive wrappers, as they are
immutable types whose equals() method fully compares their values.
Bug_Explanation: The bug was embedded in the generated code by using reference equality (==) to compare two Integer objects. This is problematic because Integer objects are cached for values between -128 and 127, so == may return true for these values. For values outside this range, == will return false even if the values are equal, demonstrating the bug.
Trigger_Explanation: The generated JUnit test cases trigger the bug by using the showBug method of the BoxedPrimitiveEqualityExample class. The first test case passes two Integer objects with values within the cached range (-128 to 127), expecting true due to reference equality. The second test case passes two Integer objects with values outside the cached range, expecting false due to reference inequality.
Bug_Trigger_Explanation: The test results confirm that the bug was triggered. The test 'testShowBugWithCachedValues' passed, indicating that comparing two Integer objects with the value 127 using '==' returned true, which is expected due to caching. The test 'testShowBugWithUncachedValues' also passed, indicating that comparing two Integer objects with the value 128 using '==' returned false, which is expected because 128 is not cached. These results demonstrate the bug behavior as described.
